content.overview: BNS s. 50 — Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of the abettor.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of the abettor. BNS restatement of IPC 110. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 110. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 50 is the rule on “Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of the abettor”. The section provides that whoever abets the commission of an offence shall, if the person abetted does the act with a different intention or knowledge from that of the abettor, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence which would have been committed if the act had been done with the intention or knowledge of the abettor and with no other. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 50 exists so that “Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of the abettor” has a closed legal test in Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: The inchoate trio. Abetment now covers extra-territorial aid; conspiracy and attempt sit next to it.

The provision in detail
50. Whoever abets the commission of an offence shall, if the person abetted does the act with a different intention or knowledge from that of the abettor, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence which would have been committed if the act had been done with the intention or knowledge of the abettor and with no other

learningObjectives: Understand the rule under BNS s. 50 when the perpetrator acts with a different intention from the abettor.
Analyze why the abettor's liability is strictly measured by his own state of mind.
Apply the principle to scenarios involving innocent or differently motivated agents.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 50 provides that whoever abets the commission of an offence shall, if the person abetted does the act with a different intention or knowledge from that of the abettor, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence which would have been committed if the act had been done with the intention or knowledge of the abettor, and with no other.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: An abettor's culpability is judged strictly according to his own mens rea, not according to the independent, uncommunicated state of mind of the person he abets.
statutoryFramework: Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt, BNS s. 50 (corresponding to IPC s. 110).
Scenario: The person abetted carries out the act, but with a different intention or knowledge.
Measure of punishment: Punished for the offence that would have occurred if done with the abettor's intention/knowledge.
Negative constraint: 'and with no other' — abettor cannot be subjected to a higher penalty based on the perpetrator's worse state of mind.
essentialIngredients: An offence was abetted by the accused.
The physical act was performed by the person abetted.
The person abetted acted with a different intention or knowledge.
The abettor is punished solely on the basis of his own intention or knowledge.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 50 protects the fundamental tenet of individual subjective guilt. If A instigates B to deliver a beating to C intending only simple hurt (s. 115), but B harbors a secret personal grudge and deliberately stabs C to death with murderous intent, A cannot be convicted of murder under this section (subject to s. 51 probable consequence). A is judged solely according to his own intention — voluntarily causing hurt. Conversely, if A instigates B to kill C, but B merely inflicts a light scratch and leaves, A's inchoate liability for instigating murder remains governed by his own murderous intention under s. 55.
examples: Teaching example (Different intent): A, with the intention of causing simple hurt to Z, instigates B to strike Z. B, harboring an undisclosed blood feud against Z, shoots Z dead. Under s. 50, A's liability is measured by the offence which would have occurred if B had acted with A's intention (simple hurt), unless murder was a probable consequence under s. 51.

Teaching example (Perjury with different belief): A instigates B to give evidence which A knows to be false. B gives the evidence, mistakenly believing it to be true. B commits no perjury, but A is punished under s. 50 as if B had given it with A's knowledge of falsity.
distinctions: Section 50 vs Section 51: Section 50 deals with different INTENTIONS in doing the act abetted; Section 51 deals with a completely DIFFERENT ACT being done.
Subjective liability vs Constructive extension: Section 50 restricts liability to the abettor's own mens rea.
problemApplication: Issue: What is the liability of an abettor who supplied an unlabelled bottle of sedative to a caregiver intending to induce sleep, where the caregiver knew it was lethal poison and administered it to murder the patient?
Rule: BNS s. 50 measures the abettor's liability solely by the intention and knowledge of the abettor, and with no other.
Application: The abettor intended only an unlawful administration of a stupefying substance. The caregiver's independent murderous intent cannot be transferred to the abettor under s. 50.
Conclusion: The abettor is punished for the offence corresponding to his own intention (administering drug), not for murder.
